The Metaverse leverages multiple technologies, including digital twins, blockchain, artificial intelligence, extended reality, and edge computing to realize the seamless connectivity and interaction between both worlds: physical and virtual. Artificial Intelligence (AI) empow- ers intelligent decisions in such complex dynamic environments. More specifically, Re- inforcement Learning (RL) is uniquely effective in the context of Metaverse applications due to the natural process of learning through interaction and its modeling of sequential decision making, allowing it to be flexible, dynamic, and able to discover complex strate- gies and emergent behavior in complicated environments where programming explicit rules is impractical. Although multiple works have explored the research on the Metaverse and AI-based applications, there remains a significant gap in the literature that addresses the contribution of RL algorithms within the Metaverse. Therefore, this review presents a comprehensive overview of RL algorithms for Metaverse applications. We examine the architecture of Metaverse networks, the role of RL in enhancing virtual interactions, and the potential for transferring learned behaviors to real-world applications. Furthermore, we categorize the key challenges, opportunities, and research directions associated with deploying RL in the Metaverse. While DTs are a foundational component of the Metaverse, the two concepts remain distinct: the Meta- verse refers to a persistent, shared, and immersive environment that integrates multiple DTs alongside human avatars and AI agents into a cohesive socio-technical system. In contrast, a virtual environment does not necessarily correspond to real-world objects or systems; instead, it can represent fully synthetic worlds that facilitate experimentation, exploration of new phenomena, or scenarios beyond the constraints of physical reality (Negri and Abdel- Aty 2023; Sai et al. 2024). As such, the Metaverse is increasingly envisioned as the next evolutionary stage of the Internet, enabling individuals and organizations to interact through immersive digital counterparts in a parallel, fully virtualized ecosystem (Wang et al. 2023a). The Metaverse is the next frontier in digital exploration, where individuals can virtu- ally interact, work, play, and create virtual worlds. Realizing this new paradigm requires the integration and collaboration of enabling technologies such as blockchain (Haber and Stornetta 1991; Nakamoto 2008), artificial intelligence (McCarthy et al. 2006; Fadhel et al. 2024), extended reality (Sutherland et al. 1965; Cardenas-Robledo et al. 2022), and edge computing (Satyanarayanan 2017). Within AI advancements, RL is a machine learning (ML) technique where an agent learns optimal behaviors by performing actions in an envi- ronment to maximize rewards. In supervised ML problems, labeled data guides the learning process. However, RL relies on interactions with the environment and feedback in the form of rewards or penalties. Reinforcement learning is more challenging than the traditional ML model because it involves exploration, stability, and reward modeling (Li 2017). With their recent success, RL-based models have been widely adopted across various domains, such as video games (ElDahshan et al. 2022), robotics (Kober et al. 2013), and autonomous driving (Kiran et al. 2021). Furthermore, they have also been adopted in diverse industrial applications such as Netflix, Amazon, Spotify, etc, to enhance their recommender systems and deliver personalized user recommendations (Kou et al. 2024). This work provides the first review to explore both how RL can enhance Metaverse experiences and how the Metaverse itself can serve as a testbed for real-world RL challenges. This work provides a detailed discussion of simulation platforms tailored for RL-driven Metaverse applications; an area that remains underexplored in existing literature. The review also introduces the use of human feedback as a key mechanism for creating adap- tive, safe, and intelligent agents within immersive environments. In addition to surveying current developments, this review analyzes the challenges and identifies potential research directions for expanding the RL-based Metaverse ecosystem. By integrating these dimensions, the study presents a holistic view of the state of RL in the context of Metaverse technologies. Focusing specifically on literature at the intersection of RL and the Metaverse, the review systematically categorizes existing work based on how RL contributes to different compo- nents of Metaverse architecture. It offers insights into how RL algorithms are being adapted and optimized to tackle the unique challenges posed by distributed virtual environments. The exploration is guided by two main research questions: ● RQ1: How has reinforcement learning been integrated into various modules of the Metaverse? How can different RL algorithms enhance its components, processes, and services? ● RQ2: How can the Metaverse serve as a platform to improve the performance and ap- plicability of RL algorithms in real-world contexts? To address these questions, the literature is examined in terms of the RL algorithms used, the roles of RL agents, and the types of problems they are designed to solve. Special attention is given to the complexity and high-dimensional nature of Metaverse environments, empha- sizing the value of simulation platforms that offer researchers detailed data access and high degrees of control and customization within virtual environments. Furthermore, our review analyzes how RL algorithms, agent roles, and problem settings intersect with Metaverse requirements. We emphasize on the role of simulation platforms, with their fine-grained control and human-in-the-loop integration, and the broader ways in which RL emerges as a core enabler of adaptive, interactive, and transferable intelligence within immersive virtual environments. 1.4 Paper structure The remainder of the paper is outlined as follows. RL algorithms can be distinguished by the aspects of the underlying MDP they represent and the approaches used to update the representations during the learning phase (Ribeiro 2002). In RL, the terms model-free and model-based are used to indicate whether, during training or testing, the agent utilizes a prediction of the change in the environments. Model-based methods are difficult to implement for higher-dimensional state spaces or MDPs where the transition probabilities and reward functions are unknown or computationally challenging. For these rea- sons, RL research in Metaverse systems uses state-of-the-art RL algorithms that aim to balance the amount of state exploration and the exploitation of previous knowledge to approximate opti- mal solutions. Model-based RL algorithms In model-based RL algorithms, the agent relies on an explicit model of the environment comprised of the transition dynamics and reward function. Thus, the RL agent learns to predict the reward of its actions’ outcomes and greedily chooses the action that maximizes its expected reward. If S and A are finite and discrete, and γ <1, then dynamic programming using Value Iteration, Q-Value Iteration, or Policy Iteration algorithms may be used to solve the MDP. Such RL agents are well-suited for scenarios where there is full knowl- edge of the environment and the effect of all the actions within the environment. Model-based RL algorithms are often used for static or fixed environments where agents can effectively learn and formulate future actions (Polydoros and Nalpantidis 2017). Model-free RL algorithms In model-free RL algorithms, the agent builds its learning experi- ence by performing actions and observing their rewards without constructing an explicit model of the environment dynamics. These algorithms may sample from their experience memory but do not generate predictions of the next state or next reward. They use the accumulated experience to learn a policy or strategy function, which decides actions aimed at optimizing rewards. Monte Carlo methods can be used to estimate Vπ(s) and Qπ(s,a) by iteratively sampling actions and the consequent rewards, however, they would require a computationally unrealistic amounts of data. Therefore, other RL algorithms such as SARSA, Q-learning, and Actor-Critic methods are favored for having higher computational efficiency given that they experience sufficient data. Exploration–exploitation dilemma A central challenge in RL is the exploration–exploitation dilemma, which refers to the trade-off between choosing actions that yield high expected rewards based on current knowledge (exploitation) and selecting actions that may lead to new knowledge and potentially greater long-term rewards (exploration). Exploitation focuses on leveraging pre- viously visited states to maximize immediate rewards by selecting likely sub-optimal actions. However, this strategy risks premature convergence to suboptimal policies if the agent fails to adequately explore the environment. Alternatively, exploration involves selecting actions with uncertain outcomes, which may initially result in lower rewards but can help uncover better policies in the long run. In order to circumvent such dilemma, RL agents use methods such as ϵ -greedy, soft max action selection, Thompson sampling, and Upper Confidence Bound (UCB), each offering different mechanisms to trade off short-term gains for long-term performance. For example, Q-learning uses a parameter ϵ to determine the probability of selecting a random action or greedily choosing the action based on the current best estimate of the Q-value function. 1 3 34 Page 14 of 58 N. Policy-based RL algorithms Policy-based RL methods learn a parameterized policy π directly, optimizing it to maximize expected cumulative rewards. These methods are espe- cially useful in environments with high-dimensional or continuous action spaces. Some examples of policy-based RL algorithms include traditional Policy Gradient and its faster- converging counterparts, Natural Policy Gradient, REINFORCE, Trust Region Policy Opti- mization (TRPO), Deterministic Policy Gradient (DPG), and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). Value-based RL algorithms Value-based methods in RL approximate optimal value functions of the MDP without explicitly storing a policy function. As noted earlier, the policy function is implicit and can be derived directly from the value function by picking the action with the best value. Some examples of value-based RL algorithms include Temporal-Difference Learn- ing (Q-learning and SARSA), Deep Q-Networks (DQN), Double Deep Q-Networks (Double DQN), and Dueling Deep Q-Networks (Dueling DQN). These methods are effective in discrete action spaces and can leverage experience replay for sample efficiency. Actor-critic RL algorithms Actor-critic architectures for RL merge both value-based and pol- icy-based methods. The algorithms learn two models: 1) the actor agent that learns the policy and 2) the critic agent that learns to evaluate the actor and is then used to improve the policy. There are several types of Actor-Critic algorithms, including Advantage Actor-Critic (A2C), Asynchronous Advantage Actor-Critic (A3C), Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG), Twin Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (TD3), and Soft Actor-Critic (SAC). These 1 3 Reinforcement learning and the Metaverse: a symbiotic collaboration Page 15 of 58 34 hybrid architectures are particularly powerful in continuous action domains and benefit from both stability and flexibility. Deep reinforcement learning Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) integrates RL with deep learning to enable agents to make decisions in complex, high-dimensional environments (Wong et al. 2023). Traditional RL methods, such as tabular Q-learning, work well in environments with small and discrete state spaces. However, in real-world applications such as, robotic control, game playing, or autonomous driving, the state space can be enormous or continuous, making tabular methods infeasible. DRL uses neural networks as function approximators to estimate value functions or policies, allowing the agent to handle high-dimensional inputs and generalize across similar states. Deep Q-Network (DQN) is a classic example of DRL which uses a convo- lutional neural network to approximate the Q-value function. Quantum reinforcement learning Quantum Reinforcement Learning (QRL) enhances clas- sical RL by leveraging principles of quantum computing, such as superposition, entanglement, and quantum interference, to improve learning efficiency, scalability, and decision-making performance. QRL models, adopt hybrid quantum-classical architectures, in which variational quantum circuits (VQCs) serve as function approximators for policies or value functions (See- tohul et al. 2024). VQCs are parameterized quantum circuits composed of quantum rotation gates (Rx, Ry, Rz) and entanglement gates (CNOT or CZ) that connect qubits. These circuits are trained similarly to neural networks by adjusting the parameters that dictate the rotation angles using gradient-based optimization techniques. The entanglement between qubits allows the quantum model to capture complex correlations between input features that may be diffi- cult to learn with classical models. These quantum models leverage phenomena like superposi- tion, entanglement, and quantum interference to enable richer representations and more efficient exploration of the state-action space. Quantum models, which operate on probability amplitudes, are naturally suited for capturing features with inherent uncertainty. QRL also enables more efficient exploration of the action space by leveraging quantum superposition, allowing agents to evaluate multiple strategies simultaneously. Moreover, quantum entanglement allows QRL- based systems to uncover and exploit complex correlations between parameters that classical models may struggle to represent. QRL also facilitates scalable learning across multiple agents and environments by supporting parallel policy updates and coordinated behavior through quan- tum-enhanced communication. Resource management encompasses the efficient allocation of communication channels, storage, computational power resources, and physical positions of the enablers. Synchronization activities go hand-in-hand with the existing resource management activities while adding concerns regarding the efficient col- lection of data, the size of information to transfer, and how often to transfer it. In the litera- ture, RL approaches have been proposed to perform the different resource management and synchronization tasks in the Metaverse enabler space with the goals of minimizing latency, maximizing throughput, and maximizing the quality of experience of the user. These tasks include: a) wireless resource management, b) computing resource management, c) mobil- ity management, d) quantization, and e) sampling. For instance, hier- archical multi-agent RL has been applied in education to coordinate intelligent non-player characters (NPCs) and learning companions (Hare and Tang 2023). Such techniques are not only transferable within the educational space but also hold promise for other complex human-centric tasks, such as dynamic traffic moderation in virtual cities (Li et al. 2025b) or adaptive healthcare support within human digital twins (Chen et al. 2024b). Despite this potential, most studies rely on predefined or simulated quality-of-experience (QoE) metrics to evaluate their systems. Only a limited number integrate human evaluators to directly assess realism, engagement, or usability (Pu et al. 2024; Jin et al. 2022; Wu et al. 2025). The use of RL as a surrogate for human behavior in Metaverse game design illus- trates both the practicality and creativity of this approach: it allows researchers to approxi- mate costly and time-consuming user studies while still generating rules and dynamics that reflect plausible human decision-making (Pu et al. 2024). Similarly, specialized use-cases such as RL-driven fuzzing (Li et al. 2023b) demonstrate how RL can augment or replace metaheuristics (e.g., genetic algorithms) by adaptively modeling their mutation, crossover, or branching strategies to reduce inefficiency. Looking ahead, future research should explore hybrid frameworks where human feed- back and RL agents co-evolve, enabling systems that learn from both simulated environ- ments and lived user interactions. Cross-domain generalization of RL policies, where solutions developed for education, gaming, or healthcare seamlessly extend into adjacent domains, remains a key challenge. Equally important is the development of richer evalu- ation metrics that go beyond technical performance (e.g., latency or accuracy) to capture subjective aspects such as user trust, perceived fairness, and long-term engagement. By embedding the human perspective more deeply into the design loop, RL-driven Metaverse systems can move closer to being adaptive, trustworthy, and genuinely user-centric. 4 Metaverse RL applications for real-life The Metaverse offers a comprehensive virtual environment for training RL algorithms where RL agents can undergo extensive training in a controlled, simulated setting that closely mimics real-world conditions. These challenges span multiple domains, including the intricacies of designing effective reward functions and the scalability and computational burden of training agents across vast and dynamic virtual environments, while ensuring that models generalize well from simulated to real-world applications. This section explores the key hurdles faced by researchers working at the intersection of RL and the Metaverse, highlighting the technical, ethical, and practical obstacles that must be addressed to unlock the full potential of an RL-empowered Metaverse (Table 6). 5.1 Training performance Design and optimization of reward functions are key issues when developing RL-based applications for the Metaverse. In traditional RL, an agent learns to navigate an environment and make decisions based on carefully crafted reward signals. However, in the complex and dynamic environments of the Metaverse, defining success and measuring performance can be exceptionally difficult. The reward signals in such environments may often be sparse or poorly aligned with the true objectives, necessitating reward shaping (Ng et al. 1999). While reward shaping can make learning more efficient, it also introduces the risk of spuri- ous correlations and reward hacking, where agents exploit specific aspects of the reward structure to achieve high rewards without actually fulfilling the intended tasks (Skalse et al. 2022). This misalignment between the reward and the desired outcome poses a significant obstacle in deploying RL effectively in the Metaverse (Kaufmann et al. 2023). Furthermore, RL agents often require millions of samples to learn an effective policy, making the process computationally expensive and potentially impractical, in real-life scenarios, especially, in the interactive and immersive settings of the Metaverse. 5.2 Scalability and computational complexity Deep RL demonstrated remarkable success across various domains, including Go and Atari games. However, these successes are often limited to single-task performance, where an agent is trained exclusively on each task. A major challenge arises when these methods are simultaneously scaled to handle multiple tasks (Espeholt et al. 2018). Current state- of-the-art techniques like A3C and UNREAL require substantial computational resources, sometimes processing up to a billion frames over several days to master a single domain. Training complex RL algorithms in the Meta- verse provides the advantage of experimenting with extreme scenarios without the risks and constraints of real-world testing. It accelerates the development cycle and reduces costs compared to traditional, resource-intensive methods. However, challenges such as the sim- to-real gap can arise when transitioning from virtual to physical environments, due to the dynamic and unpredictable nature of the real-world. 5.4 Model generalization One of the significant limitations of traditional RL models is their ability to generalize across different environments and conditions. While RL methods are designed to optimize policies based on expected cumulative rewards within a given MDP framework, they often struggle when faced with uncertainties such as random perturbations, model inaccuracies, or adver- sarial conditions. Furthermore, these methods rely on recurrent neural networks (RNNs) or CNN to process sequential inputs and maintain state information. However, these architec- tures can struggle with long-term dependencies and scaling issues (Hu et al. 2024a). 5.5 Model transparency Currently, the RL models developed for Metaverse applications work in a black-box man- ner that lacks interpretability. These models make decisions based on complex calculations across multiple neural network layers; however, they are unable to justify their decisions to humans, including domain experts and even the engineers who designed the systems. This poses significant challenges when such models are deployed in critical domains, especially in healthcare or self-driving cars. Furthermore, since it is difficult to interpret how decisions are made, it becomes challenging to ensure that the models adhere to ethical guidelines and are not biased. Additionally, due to lack of interpretability, it is challenging to identify errors or suboptimal behavior in RL models. 5.6 Performance metrics Performance metrics are indispensable for evaluating and optimizing Metaverse applica- tions, ensuring they meet the high demands of seamless and efficient user experiences. These metrics provide essential insights into various aspects of system performance and reliability. For example, latency metrics like total latency, uplink delay, and downlink delay are vital for real-time interactions and smooth virtual experiences. Throughput and reliabil- ity assess the system’s capacity to handle data traffic and maintain consistent performance under varying conditions. Visual and sensory quality metrics, such as successful frames per second (FPS), are crucial for ensuring immersive and fluid virtual environments. Further- more, metrics such as Mean Squared Error (MSE) and Mean Absolute Error (MAE) are used to evaluate the performance of ML models. Similarly, for RL models, Convergence time, reward, etc., are used to measure the agent’s ability to learn and adapt to the environ- ment. Although various Metaverse applications have unique requirements and challenges, it 1 3 Reinforcement learning and the Metaverse: a symbiotic collaboration Page 45 of 58 34 is necessary to adopt a diverse set of metrics tailored to specific scenarios beyond the com- munications aspects of the Metaverse. There is still a need to establish common or standard- ized performance metrics for fair comparison and evaluation. 5.7 Security The Metaverse, as a complex and immersive virtual environment, introduces several sig- nificant cybersecurity challenges that need to be addressed to ensure the safety and security of its users and infrastructure. The Metaverse faces multiple security challenges, which primarily include: data integrity, identity verification, and digital identity management (Awadallah et al. 2024). Data tampering and man-in-the-middle attacks can distort the digi- tal twin’s representation and lead to flawed decisions. Furthermore, the reliance on custom- izable digital avatars and the potential for deepfake technology to create highly realistic but fraudulent representations of users complicates verifying true identities. This leads to identity theft and impersonation, where malicious actors could deceive others, leading to unauthorized access, financial fraud, and severe privacy breaches. Additionally, integrat- ing biometric data, such as facial features and behavioral patterns, in VR technology raises concerns about the security of sensitive personal information. If authentication mechanisms are compromised, it could result in significant privacy violations and misuse of biometric data. The dynamic nature of the Metaverse is vulnerable to advanced cyber threats like Denial of Service (DoS) attacks, which could disrupt services and cause significant down- time. Furthermore, the use of AI techniques by malicious actors to launch automated attacks that can evade detection, known as Advanced Persistent Threats (Alshamrani et al. 2019), poses a severe threat to the Metaverse’s security. Traditional cybersecurity measures that rely on static approaches, such as firewalls and antivirus software, are insufficient to counter these advanced threats, particularly in the face of zero-day attacks that exploit previously unknown vulnerabilities (Ahmad et al. 2023). RL systems, which are critical in managing these complex environments, are also vulnerable to a range of security threats that can compromise the performance and integrity of the systems. RL models can be compromised through data poisoning or adversarial attacks, leading to incorrect actions that could have severe consequences, especially in critical applications like autonomous vehicles (Lei et al. 2023). 5.8 Privacy concerns RL systems can be exploited to expose sensitive information due to the dynamic and exten- sive data collection involved in training. Privacy attacks may involve inferring private information from the collected data or exploiting vulnerabilities in data transfer and stor- age systems. Several techniques, such as differential privacy and encryption, are employed to safeguard data, while federated learning protects individual privacy by decentralizing the learning process. Most of the studies performed for Metaverse applications overlooked the security and privacy concerns associated with their proposed models. Therefore, future studies should also focus on safeguarding their proposed methods from potential security and privacy concerns. 1 3 34 Page 46 of 58 N. Elsokkary et al. Such unique ethical challenges must be addressed at multiple levels, from system design to user interaction. One of the primary ethical considerations in developing RL systems for the Metaverse is establishing a robust regulatory framework. Governments and regulatory bodies need to define clear guidelines and standards to ensure that ethical practices are embedded into the development process of RL engines, tools, and frameworks (Sami et al. 2024). For example, integrating ethical regulations directly into the design phase can prevent potential misuse of RL technologies, such as biased decision-making algorithms or unfair reward structures that might benefit certain groups of users over others. The design of RL systems in the Metaverse should adhere to ethical principles prioritizing user well-being, and ensuring that RL-driven experiences do not exploit psychological vulnerabilities, such as addiction or compulsive behavior. Developers must also obtain informed consent from users, particu- larly when RL systems modify or influence their behavior (Lee and Hu-Au 2021). Ensuring ethical consideration can create a Metaverse that is innovative, engaging, and aligned with ethical principles that safeguard the interests and well-being of all users. 6 Research direction As the Metaverse continues to evolve, the integration of reinforcement learning offers vast potential but also presents significant challenges that require careful design mechanisms and innovative solutions. This section discusses possible future directions to address the key limitations posed by integrating RL techniques and applications within the Metaverse. Figure 8 shows the potential research directions for the challenges faced by RL-based Metaverse. 1 3 Reinforcement learning and the Metaverse: a symbiotic collaboration Page 47 of 58 34 6.1 Reinforcement learning from human feedback Human-in-the-loop (HITL) RL integrates human judgments, preferences, or corrections into learning. By leveraging human expertise, RL algorithms can be guided toward desired behaviors more efficiently than relying on predefined reward functions or exploration strate- gies, particularly in complex environments where specifying exact reward functions can be challenging. HITL RL accelerates learning and improves the alignment of AI systems with human values and expectations (Xie et al. 2024; Wu et al. 2023b). Traditional RL methods often require extensive interactions with the environment to learn effective policies, which can be computationally expensive and time-consuming. Human feedback can help bridge this gap by providing high-level guidance or corrections enabling the agent to learn more effectively from fewer interactions. However, integrating human feedback into RL algo- rithms can be noisy, subjective, and inconsistent, which introduces biases or errors into the learning process. Therefore, the feedback should be consistent, reliable, and accurate to reflect the desired behavior. Furthermore, the integration process must be carefully designed to balance human input with the agent’s learning, preventing over-reliance on feedback that might limit the agent’s ability to explore and learn independently. The dynamic nature of the Metaverse adds complexity to the collection and integration of feedback. Additionally, addressing privacy and ethical concerns related to collecting and utilizing human feedback will be essential to maintaining user trust and ensuring the responsible development of Metaverse technologies. Therefore, this presents a promising area for future research in the field. 6.2 Meta layer and physical layer As represented in Sect. 3, the majority of existing research is focused on the Enabler layer, often neglecting other critical layers within the framework. While enablers play a founda- tional role in ensuring the seamless operation of Metaverse environments, the meta layer and physical layer have received comparatively little attention. For instance, Fig. 5 shows that over 80% of the works focus on the enabler layer, whereas only a small fraction address the virtual and physical layers. Therefore, future research should prioritize the unexplored layers to enhance both physical and virtual experiences and achieve seamless integration. 6.3 Decentralized RL approaches Future research should focus on decentralized learning approaches, where the learning pro- cess is distributed across multiple agents or nodes. This method can reduce the computa- tional burden on a single entity and improve the scalability of RL systems. Furthermore, Quantum computing can drastically accelerate RL computations, enabling faster training and more complex models. Quantum-enhanced RL algorithms could leverage quantum theory to explore and exploit large state and action spaces more efficiently than classical approaches. Moreover, employing decentralized agents enhances the security of the Meta- verse by eliminating the potential risks associated with centralized systems, such as single point of failure. 1 3 34 Page 48 of 58 N. Elsokkary et al. 6.4 Domain randomization in the Metaverse To mitigate the issues of model generalization and Meta-to-Real transfer, techniques like domain randomization can be employed to enhance the fidelity of virtual simulations. Ensuring that the virtual environment closely mirrors real-world conditions, combined with rigorous validation processes, can significantly improve the effectiveness of meta-to-real transfer. 6.5 Robust RL models Robust RL aims to address the challenges of Meta-to-Real transfer by extending the tra- ditional MDP framework to robust MDPs, which incorporate additional considerations to handle environmental uncertainties. Moreover, constrained MDPs are employed to ensure safety and robustness, especially in complex applications like self-driving cars, where unobserved confounders can lead to spurious correlations that negatively impact decision- making. Interestingly, Transformers can address the challenges of RNN-based modules through their self-attention mechanism, allowing them to dynamically weigh the impor- tance of different parts of the input sequence while remembering longer sequences. The self-attention mechanism enhances the model’s ability to understand and predict the future states across various RL paradigms, including offline RL, online RL, hierarchical RL, meta- RL, and multi-agent RL (MARL) (Yuan et al. 2024). For instance, in online RL and MARL, Transformers can be utilized in a pre-train-finetune manner to leverage large-scale foun- dation models (Bommasani et al. 2021) for knowledge transfer to improve generalization and performance. Moreover, Transformer-based MARL approaches, such as MADT, utilize Transformers for joint policy optimization (Yuan et al. 2024). Although much work has been done to utilize transformers-based models for RL applications, these models are yet to be adapted for Metaverse applications. Therefore, there is a need to incorporate robust transformer-based models for Metaverse applications. 6.6 AI-driven security measures The Metaverse and RL security concerns can be addressed by incorporating AI-driven cybersecurity measures that can adapt and respond to the dynamic and complex nature of the Metaverse. For instance, continuous authentication methods utilizing multi-modal biometrics—such as facial recognition, voice patterns, and behavioral biometrics—can enhance identity verification processes and prevent impersonation. These AI-based systems can detect real-time anomalies and provide more robust protection against identity theft and deepfake-related threats. Additionally, integrating blockchain technology more deeply into the Metaverse’s infrastructure can enhance the security of digital transactions and asset trad- ing. By leveraging blockchain’s decentralized and transparent nature, the risk of fraud and unauthorized access to digital assets could be minimized. There is also a need to develop more resilient and adaptive defense mechanisms to counter increasingly sophisticated cyber threats. Research into AI-powered intrusion detection systems (IDS) that can learn from emerging attack patterns and proactively defend against Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) is crucial. Moreover, enhancing the interoperability of security protocols across dif- 1 3 Reinforcement learning and the Metaverse: a symbiotic collaboration Page 49 of 58 34 ferent virtual environments within the Metaverse will be essential to ensure seamless and secure interactions between users and systems. 6.7 Privacy preserving RL solutions in the Metaverse Mitigating privacy risks in the RL-based Metaverse requires a comprehensive and multi- level approach that addresses both the inherent technical vulnerabilities and the behavioral patterns of users in these immersive environments. A privacy-by-design approach should be adopted from the beginning to ensure robust privacy protection, embedding privacy features directly into the platform’s architecture and design (Wang et al. 2023a). For example, strict data minimization and anonymization can be applied to ensure that data cannot be easily traced back to individual users if data is intercepted. Advanced cryptographic techniques and secure data-sharing methods reinforce privacy in RL algorithms within the Metaverse (Lei et al. 2023). Differential Privacy (DP) can be employed to add noise to data, ensuring individual user information remains indistinguishable within larger datasets, allowing RL models to learn effectively without compromising privacy (Lei et al. 2023). Blockchain technology provides a decentralized and transparent ledger, making it particularly relevant for RL in smart contracts and decentralized applications by ensuring data integrity and secu- rity (Xiao et al. 2023). Additionally, Federated Learning enables the training of RL models on decentralized data sources, where models are trained locally on user devices, and only the trained parameters are shared with a central server. This approach preserves user privacy while allowing RL algorithms to leverage a diverse and extensive dataset. 6.8 Explainable RL solutions Explainable Reinforcement Learning (XRL) focuses on making the decision-making pro- cesses of RL agents more transparent and explainable to enhance trust, regulatory compli- ance, and user interaction, especially in high-stakes applications like autonomous driving and healthcare. XRL provides insights into how agents make decisions, which can improve debugging, algorithm development, and user customization (Milani et al. 2024). Although multiple works have proposed and employed XRL methods (Vouros 2022; Milani et al. 2024) for RL model transparency and interpretability, there is still a need for more research on designing interpretable agents that offer transparent explanations of their behavior within the Metaverse. Such explanations are more meaningful than post-hoc explanations that only provide plausible justifications without true insight into the agent’s decision-making process (Bekkemoen 2024). Furthermore, robust XRL models should be developed that could be generalized across various domains without a specific task or particular application. 7 Conclusion The intersection of reinforcement learning and the Metaverse presents both exciting oppor- tunities and significant challenges, where RL algorithms offer promising solutions for creat- ing adaptive, intelligent systems that can enhance the user experience within the immersive virtual environments that compose the Metaverse. Therefore, this review introduces a comprehensive overview of the potentials contributions of RL to the Metaverse. It high- 1 3 34 Page 50 of 58 N. Elsokkary et al. lights key enabling technologies, such as, digital twins, blockchain, artificial intelligence, extended reality, and edge computing with a focus on the simulation software required to create complex virtual environments empowered by RL technology. The review studies the existing literature to understand the symbiotic relationship between RL and the Metaverse; examining 1) RL-based solutions for addressing common Metaverse problems such as scal- able, efficient communications, and realistic, immersive virtual experiences and 2) Meta- verse applications for providing more robust and efficient RL model training. Despite the potential of the collaboration between RL and the Metaverse, there still exists multiple challenges, such as designing effective reward mechanisms, managing the computational complexity of training agents across vast and dynamic virtual environments, ensuring secure, scalable, and generalizable RL models that are adaptable to real-life appli- cations, while addressing concerns related to model transparency and user privacy. In order to mitigate these challenges and realize the full potential of an RL-empowered Metaverse, possible research directions are introduced, such as, human-in-the-loop mechanisms, decen- tralized RL systems, privacy-preserving RL models, AI-driven security measure, and trans- parent and explainable RL models. This review serves as a foundational step in advancing the mutually-beneficial relation- ship between the Metaverse and reinforcement learning. As the Metaverse paradigm contin- ues to evolve, the ongoing advancement of RL techniques designed for the Metaverse, and those trained within it, will play a crucial role in shaping its future, driving innovation, and creating a more immersive, interactive, and user-centric virtual world. JSON: Name: hitl_constrained_ppo_sync Title: Human-in-the-loop constrained proximal policy optimization with domain randomization for sampling-rate and quantization scheduling in digital-twin synchronization for the Metaverse Short Hypothesis: Integrating a human preference-based reward model into a constrained proximal policy optimization agent trained with domain randomization for sampling-rate and quantization scheduling reduces digital-twin synchronization mean squared error by ≥20% and uplink packet rate by ≥30% versus constrained PPO trained without human feedback after sim-to-real transfer to a physical 6-DOF robotic arm. Related Work: Existing work on Metaverse synchronization and sampling-rate/quantization scheduling uses model-free DRL (e.g., PPO variants, TD3) and constrained formulations to trade off synchronization error and communication load. Prior methods incorporate domain knowledge (e.g., Jacobian-based features, prediction horizons) and constrained DRL (constraint-aware PPO, KC-TD3) to reduce packet rates while maintaining MSE. Sim2Real research applies domain randomization and digital-twin assisted training for robustness in UAVs and robotics, and human-guided RL / intervention approaches have been used to accelerate policy learning in control tasks. Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) and AI-generated feedback (RLAIF) have been demonstrated for language and policy alignment but have not been combined systematically with constrained DRL for sampling/quantization scheduling. Limitations across prior approaches include: (1) reward functions that do not reflect human perceptual preferences or QoE, (2) absence of integrated human preference models for synchronization trade-offs, (3) limited ablation of the joint effect of domain randomization and human feedback on sim-to-real transfer, and (4) few works evaluate constrained, human-in-the-loop RL on real robotic hardware for digital-twin synchronization. Abstract: We address the problem of scheduling sampling rates and data quantization for digital-twin synchronization in Metaverse applications under stringent communication constraints. We propose a method that combines constrained proximal policy optimization (C-PPO) with a human preference-derived reward model and domain-randomized simulation training. Human annotators provide pairwise judgments over replayed synchronization rollouts to train a compact reward network that captures perceptual quality and task-relevance. C-PPO optimizes sampling and quantization actions subject to explicit bandwidth and latency constraints while domain randomization over physics, sensor noise, and network impairments improves robustness for sim-to-real transfer. The main contributions are (1) a pipeline integrating human preference learning with constraint-aware DRL for synchronization control, (2) an empirical evaluation of the joint effect of human feedback and domain randomization on sim-to-real transfer to a physical 6-DOF robotic arm, and (3) ablation studies quantifying the value of each component on synchronization MSE, packet rate, latency, and subjective QoE. We expect the proposed approach to deliver lower synchronization error and reduced bandwidth usage compared to constraint-aware RL without human guidance. Experiments: Datasets and platforms: (1) Simulation: NVIDIA Isaac Sim environment modeling a 6-DOF robotic arm (Franka Emika Panda) with a digital twin; simulated tasks: periodic joint-space trajectories (1,000 distinct trajectories, each 20s long) and pick-and-place episodes (500 episodes). Domain randomization ranges: friction ±30%, link mass ±20%, sensor noise Gaussian σ_joint ∈ [0.001,0.01] rad, packet loss ∈ [0%,20%], network delay ∈ [0,150] ms. (2) Real-world: physical Franka Emika Panda executing 50 validation trajectories and 30 pick-and-place trials in lab network conditions. (3) Human feedback dataset: 500 pairwise comparisons collected from 30 human evaluators on 10s recorded synchronization rollouts sampled from simulation and early transfer trials. Baselines: (A) constrained PPO without human reward (C-PPO-plain), (B) KC-TD3 (knowledge-assisted TD3), (C) domain-randomized TD3 without human feedback, (D) heuristic scheduler (fixed sampling period and quantization levels tuned to average bandwidth), (E) oracle (policy with access to ground-truth real-state; upper bound). Proposed method: Human-in-the-loop constrained PPO with learned preference reward (HiTL-C-PPO) trained with domain randomization. Evaluation metrics: synchronization mean squared error (MSE) between physical state and digital twin, average uplink packet rate (packets/s), end-to-end latency (ms), convergence episodes to within 5% of peak reward, subjective Mean Opinion Score (MOS) from 20 raters on 30 transferred rollouts, and sim-to-real performance gap (relative MSE increase on real vs simulated evaluation). Experimental protocol: train all RL agents for 1e6 environment steps with 5 independent random seeds; use same network architectures across PPO variants (actor 2-layer 256 units, critic 2-layer 256 units). Reward model training: train a neural reward network (two-layer 128 units) on the 500 pairwise labels via Bradley–Terry / logistic pairwise loss; freeze reward model for RL training. Ablations: (1) remove human preference reward (compare HiTL-C-PPO vs C-PPO-plain), (2) remove domain randomization (train HiTL-C-PPO with nominal sim only), (3) replace constraints with penalty term, (4) vary number of human labels (500, 250, 100) and evaluate sensitivity. Statistical analysis: report mean ± std over seeds; perform paired t-tests (α=0.05) between proposed method and each baseline on primary metrics (MSE, packet rate). Hardware: training on a workstation with 2x NVIDIA A5000 GPUs, 128GB RAM. Real-world safety: run deployment trials under supervised safety protocols. Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical failure modes: (1) mis-specified human-derived reward model leading to reward hacking or policies that optimize perceptual score but worsen control stability; (2) insufficient domain randomization coverage resulting in large sim-to-real gaps; (3) noisy, inconsistent, or biased human preference labels degrading reward model quality. Data and evaluation biases: human raters demographic or expertise bias may skew the learned reward toward specific preferences; limited trajectory diversity may bias generalization. Scalability and compute: training C-PPO with domain randomization and human reward requires substantial compute; real-time inference constraints on embedded metaverse edge nodes may limit deployment of large networks. Safety and real-world hazards: transferring policies that alter sampling/quantization may inadvertently degrade closed-loop control and trigger unsafe robot motions; real-world trials require human supervision. Limits to generalization: method is validated on a 6-DOF manipulator—results may not transfer directly to other robot morphologies, mobile agents, or multi-agent synchronization without re-training and additional human feedback. Privacy and collection risk: collecting human preference data raises consent and privacy requirements. Regulatory and interpretability limits: resulting policies may be difficult to interpret, complicating certification in safety-critical Metaverse applications.
